'''Daniel Zissel Freedman''' (born 1939 in [[Hartford, Connecticut]]) is an American [[theoretical physicist]]. He is an emeritus Professor of [[Physics]] and [[Applied Mathematics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), and is currently a visiting professor at [[Stanford University]]. He is mainly known for his work in [[supergravity]]. He is a member of the U. S. [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|title=News from the National Academy of Sciences|date=April 26, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021|quote=Newly elected members and their affiliations at the time of election are:  ...  Freedman, Daniel Z.; professor emeritus of applied mathematics and physics, department of mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology; visiting professor, Institute for Theoretical Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, Calif.}}</ref>

==Education==
Daniel Freedman completed his undergraduate degree from [[Wesleyan University]] and completed his Ph.D. from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 1964. In 1967–68, Freedman was a member of the School of Natural Sciences at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], and returned subsequently in 1973–74 and 1986–87.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/daniel-freedman|title=Daniel Freedman|website=Institute for Advanced Study|language=en|access-date=2019-08-06}}</ref> He was appointed Professor of [[Applied Mathematics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) in 1980 and joint Professor of [[Physics]] in 2001. Before joining MIT, he was a professor at [[Stony Brook University]].

==Supergravity==
In 1976, Daniel Z. Freedman codiscovered (with [[Sergio Ferrara]] and [[Peter van Nieuwenhuizen]]) [[supergravity]]. Freedman and van Nieuwenhuizen were on the faculty of the [[Stony Brook University]]. Supergravity generalizes Einstein's theory of general relativity by incorporating the then-new idea of [[supersymmetry]]. In the following decades it had implications for physics beyond the [[Standard Model]], for [[superstring theory]] and for mathematics. For his work on supergravity, Freedman, a former Sloan and twice Guggenheim fellow, received in 1993 the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] and Prize, in 2006 the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]],<ref>[http://insti.physics.sunysb.edu/ITP/awards/2006Heineman.html Discovery of Supergravity at Stony Brook Recognized by the APS Dannie Heineman Prize].</ref> in 2016 the [[Majorana Medal]]<ref name="DZF@MIT">[http://web.mit.edu/physics/people/faculty/freedman_daniel.html Daniel Z. Freedman at MIT].</ref> and in 2019 the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]],<ref>{{cite news |title='Supergravity' Theorists Win $3 Million Physics Breakthrough Prize |author=Mike Wall |url=https://www.space.com/supergravity-discovery-physics-breakthrough-prize.html |publisher=[[Space.com]] |date=August 6, 2019 |access-date=August 6, 2019}}</ref> in each case together with his codiscoverers Sergio Ferrara and Peter van Nieuwenhuizen. Freedman also gave the 2002 Andrejewski Lectures in Mathematical Physics  at the [[Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences]] in [[Leipzig]].<ref name="DZF@MIT"/>

==Research interests==
Daniel Freedman is a professor at  MIT. His research is in [[quantum field theory]], [[quantum gravity]], and [[superstring theory]] with an emphasis on the role of [[supersymmetry]]. He is also noted for proposing in 1974 what would become known as [[Coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering]] (CEvNS), which was experimentally confirmed in 2017.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freedman |first=Daniel Z. |date=1974-03-01 |title=Coherent effects of a weak neutral current |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.9.1389 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=1389–1392 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.9.1389 |bibcode=1974PhRvD...9.1389F |issn=0556-2821|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Adamski |first1=S. |title=First detection of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering on germanium |date=2024-06-19 |eprint=2406.13806 |last2=Ahn |first2=M. |last3=Barbeau |first3=P. S. |last4=Belov |first4=V. |last5=Bernardi |first5=I. |last6=Bock |first6=C. |last7=Bolozdynya |first7=A. |last8=Bouabid |first8=R. |last9=Browning |first9=J. |class=hep-ex }}</ref> His most recent area of concentration is the [[AdS/CFT correspondence]] in which results on the strong coupling limit of certain 4-dimensional gauge theories can be obtained from calculations in classical 5-dimensional [[supergravity]].

In the academic year 1993/94 Freedman was a visiting scientist in the [[CERN]] Theory Division, [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://inspirehep.net/search?p=381056+or+375522+or+371446+or+357974+or+371951+or+376337+or+373174&f=recid |title=Freedman's publications authored during his sabbatical year at CERN|website=INSPIRE HEP |publisher=CERN |access-date=2019-10-17}}</ref>
